text: Least privilege is the principle; in Azure, Entra ID and Azure RBAC are the mechanisms. This lesson covers how Northbridge Retail's platform team uses Entra ID for who exists in the directory, and Azure RBAC for what each identity can do to a specific resource.

Every Azure RBAC role assignment is built from three pieces: a security principal — who or what is getting access — a role definition describing what they can do, and a scope describing where it applies. The same role means something very different depending on scope: Contributor on a whole subscription is sweeping access, while Contributor scoped to one resource group is textbook least privilege.

Microsoft Entra ID is Azure's identity directory — where users, groups, and service principals exist and authenticate, and where tenant-wide roles like Privileged Role Administrator are assigned. That's separate from access to individual Azure resources.

Resource-level access is granted from the Access control, or IAM, blade. It appears on nearly every resource, resource group, and subscription in the portal — the same screen each time, with only the scope you're standing on changing what the assignment affects.

Clicking Add role assignment opens a role picker split into job function roles for day-to-day work, and privileged administrator roles like Owner that can grant access to others — the ones that deserve extra scrutiny in a security audit.
Reading a role assignment like an auditor means checking all three parts: who has it, what it actually permits, and where it applies. Next up: the AWS equivalent, IAM roles and policies.
